sent.t: 34 years I sat beside dying people in this city.
And the hardest week of my whole life was not in anybody else's house.
It was in my mother's bedroom in March of 2015, five blocks from Woodlawn Lake.
And I was not ready, not with all those years behind me, not even close.
Here's what nobody tells you, honey.
When it's your own mother, the years don't help you.
They only let you see in slow motion every single thing you are about to do wrong.
So I made a list on the back of a receipt from the HEB on Culebra, sitting in my car with the engine off because I
couldn't walk through that door yet.
What I would never let happen to my own mother in her last week.
8 things and tonight I'm going to say them out loud because I think some of you are sitting in a car right now too.
My name is Rosa Navarro.
I have no medical training at all.
None.
I was the chaplain on the hospice team for 34 years, most of it at Alamo Home Hospice, in people's houses all over the city.
So anything about her body, anything at all, you call your hospice team, not me.
What I know is the other part, the house, the family, the things that get said and the things that never get said.
If you saw the one I did about the seven things families say at the bedside, this is the other side of it.
That one was about words, this one is about the week, and I'll be plain with you, I'm not telling you what a good daughter does.
I'm telling you what I did and what I saw in almost 3,000 houses and what I would do again.
But before the least, I want you to do something with me.
Not later.
Right now.
Think of the last ordinary Tuesday.
Not the last week.
Not the last day.
The last Tuesday when nothing was happening.
When she was in her chair and the TV was on and somebody was in the kitchen making noise with the dishes.
Who was in the room?
Say it in your head.
Not who came to visit in the final week.
Who was in the room on an ordinary Tuesday?
Because that's the whole video.
Everything I'm going to tell you tonight is about that room on that Tuesday and what the last week does to it.
Most families, when I ask a question, go quiet.
And then they say something like, I was at work, or my sister was there, I think.
Honey, that's not a confession.
That's just a lie.
But the last week is built out of ordinary Tuesdays.
And if you want to change the last week, you start with a Tuesday.
Okay, eight things.
Let's go.
Number one, I would never let my mother's room fill up with people who came to see themselves.
Mr.
Delgado was a veteran of the Korean War, from over by Kelly Field.
I sat with him in 2003, in a little house on Guadalupe Street.
And by his last week, that living room had more people in it than a wedding.
Cousins he hadn't seen in 20 years.
A neighbor who brought a cake and stayed four hours.
A man in a nice shirt who stood in the doorway and told everybody about his own father's passing for 40 minutes.
And Mr.
Delgado, who had been talking to his brother Ramiro for two days, his brother who died in 1951, turned to me and asked, very quiet, in
Spanish, Rosa, ¿quiénes son todas estas personas?
Who are all these people?
His own cousins, in his own living room.
That's what a full house does.
From the doorway it looks like love.
From the bed it feels like a crowd.
And I want to say this gently because I've been on both sides of that door.
Most of us visit so that we can be seen visiting.
We stand where the family can see us.
We bring the flowers where the flowers will be noticed.
And the person in the bed gets the leftovers of the afternoon.
Why does it happen?
Because the silence scares us.
Sitting in a quiet room with somebody who is leaving is the hardest thing a human being does.
Talking is easier, feeling the room is easier, being busy is easier.
So here's what I did.
One chair, not five, one chair beside the bed, and it stays there and whoever sits in it does not get up for anybody.
In my mother's room I put a folding chair from the hardware store on Zarzamora.
Thirty dollars, the metal kind, with the vinyl seat.
And I told my brother, this chair is the whole job.
Whoever is in the chair, that is who she is with.
And at the door I put an $18 wireless doorbell, the kind with a button and a little plug-in chime.
I put the button outside her door and the chime in the kitchen turned down low.
Why?
Because when somebody walks in, the person in the chair doesn't have to jump up and play hostess.
The chime tells the kitchen, somebody's here, come and get them.
It sounds like nothing.
It changed that house.
Tonight, go and stand in her room and count the chairs.
If there are five chairs around the bed and nobody is sitting in any of them, honey, you don't have a room.
You have a lobby.
Number two, I would never let my mother be alone at two in the morning.
Senora Ines Garza had dementia.
I visited her for 11 months out on Bandera Road, and her daughter Elena did everything, baths, food, the laundry, the appointments, the whole house, and
she did it alone because she was the only one left in San Antonio.
One night, around 9, Elena ran out to the HEB to buy coffee.
She was gone 35 minutes.
She came back, and her mother had died by herself in that room in the dark.
I got there 20 minutes later.
Elena was sitting on the front step with the bag of coffee still in her hand, and she looked at me and said, I left her
alone to buy coffee.
That sentence stayed with me for years because it wasn't true what she said.
She didn't leave her mother alone.
We did, all of us, the family, the neighbors, me, the whole world that tells a daughter that the loving thing is to do it all
yourself, night after night until you drop.
Here's what I know after 34 years, death does not keep an appointment.
It doesn't wait for the shift change or for the daughter to get back from the store.
And the families who did this well, and some did it beautifully, they all had the same thing.
They had a night list.
A night list is three names and three phone numbers on a piece of paper taped to the refrigerator with one rule.
From two in the morning until six.
Nobody is alone in that room.
It doesn't have to be family.
It can be a neighbor, a woman from the church, a cousin's husband who doesn't talk much.
That's fine.
He doesn't need to talk.
He needs to sit.
For my mother, it was Marisol on Tuesdays, my niece on Thursdays, and Ernie, my husband Ernie, on the weekend nights in the recliner with the
radio on so low you could barely hear it.
Three names.
That's all.
The cost is almost nothing.
A baby monitor.
The all-kind.
No Wi-Fi.
No camera on the internet. $40 at the store on Culebra.
A magnetic whiteboard for the refrigerator. $6.
And I wrote the three names on it in marker.
That's it.
That's the whole setup.
And here's the part nobody wants to hear.
Asking for help is not a failure.
sitting in that room alone at two in the morning night after night until you are so tired you can't see straight that's not devotion that's
how families break and a broken daughter is no good to anybody in that bed tonight before you go to sleep answer one question who is
on your 2 a.m list.
If the answer is me, that's not a plan, mija.
That's a countdown.
Number three, I would never let the papers be a mystery in that house.
Walt Pruitt was a rancher from out in Bandera, big hands, a truck that needed paint, and a daughter in Houston he hadn't talked to in
a while.
In 2011, he had one of those days, you'll hear me talk about those days in another video, where he sat up clear as morning, asked
for huevos rancheros, and called his daughter in Houston and talked to her for an hour.
His family had been paying an aid out of their own pocket for five months.
Five months.
Bathing, dressing, the bed, the supplies, the pads, all of it.
Cash every week because they thought that's what it cost.
Nobody had told them that the hospice benefit under Medicare Part A already covers the aid for the bath, the social worker, the chaplain, the hospital
bed, the wheelchair, the oxygen, the supplies, and the medications for the terminal diagnosis, with a copay of no more than $5 per prescription.
Nobody told them about respite either.
Up to five days in a facility so the family can sleep, with a 5% copay.
Nobody told them about continuous care at home during a crisis.
Nobody told them about the bereavement support for the family up to 13 months after.
Nobody told them they could change agencies once during a period.
And nobody told them about the periods themselves.
Two of 90 days and after that 60 days at a time with no limit.
I've sat at kitchen tables where a family spent $3,000, $5,000, $8,000 of their own money on things that were already paid for, not because they were careless, because
in this country we hand people a benefit and we don't hand them the words.
So here's what I would do and what I did.
One binder, a plain three ring binder from the office store, nine dollars, and on the front I wrote the name of the agency and the
night number in big letters with a marker.
Inside, the name of the hospice team, the social worker, the chaplain, the aide and her schedule, the equipment that had been delivered, and one page
called what we already paid for, where I wrote down every single thing the family had bought with their own money every week.
Because that page is where the money comes back.
Why does it work?
Because grief makes people forget and paper does not forget.
The daughter who is exhausted at 11 at night cannot remember what she was told at the kitchen table on a Tuesday in March, but the
binder can.
Tonight, go and open the drawer where the papers are.
If you don't know what's in there, honey, neither does the person who will need it at three in the morning.
And ask your hospice team this exact question.
What does the benefit already pay for and what are we paying for ourselves?
Write the answer down in the binder, not in your phone, in the binder where the whole family can see it.
Number four, I would never let my family fight in the hallway.
I was in a house in Leon Valley in 2008 with three brothers and a mother in the back bedroom.
The mother was in her last days and those three men spent two afternoons in the driveway arguing about a truck, a 1978 truck, who was
going to get it, who had paid for the tires, who had driven it to Laredo in 1994.
And one afternoon I came out of the bedroom and the mother had heard all of it through the wall.
She asked me very quiet, Rosa, are they fighting about the truck?
She was leaving in a few days and the thing she was listening to was a truck.
I want to tell you why this happens because it isn't about the truck.
It never is.
Fear comes out of people looking for something to hold on to and money is the easiest thing to hold on to.
The wheel, the house, the truck, the jewelry, the plot at the cemetery.
When a family is terrified, they start counting things.
It's the only language some people have for love But the person in that bed hears everything, everything.
The tone in the driveway, the sigh in the kitchen, the phone call in the garage.
They may not know what day it is, but they know when their children are at war.
And I have watched people hold on longer than they wanted to, because they were waiting for the house to be quiet.
So here's the rule I would put in my mother's house.
One voice, one person talks to the hospice team.
So the team is getting four different stories.
And one whiteboard on the refrigerator, $12, with three things written on it.
Who is sleeping there tonight?
What time the egg comes?
And the night number in big numbers.
Everything else, the truck, the wheel, the money, who did more, happens in the driveway, out of earshot, with the door closed.
And if there has to be a family meeting, it happens in the kitchen, before the person wakes up, with a piece of paper and a
pen, and one question, what would she want?
Not what do we want, what would she want?
Tonight, ask yourself, who is the one voice?
And if two people in your family answer at the same time, honey, you just found your first fight.
Fix it now while she can still hear you be kind.
Number five, I would never send the grandchildren out of the room.
Mrs.
Ophelia Washington sang in the choir at a Baptist church over on the east side, 60 something years in that choir.
And in her last week, her granddaughter, nine years old, missing two front teeth, stood at the foot of the bed and sang Amazing Grace off
key, every verse a little bit in the wrong place.
And Mrs.
Washington, who had not opened her eyes in two days, moved her fingers, not much, just her fingers, on the sheet in time.
Now I want you to notice what the family almost did.
The mother of that little girl had her hand on the child's shoulder ready to pull her back.
Because we do that, we send the children to another room.
We tell them go watch TV honey the grown-ups are talking.
We think we are protecting them.
We are not protecting them.
We are teaching them that this, the bed, the dying, the last week is a thing that happens behind a closed door and that they will
find out later from somebody else in a hallway at a funeral.
Children understand much more than we give them credit for and they need the goodbye as much as we do.
What they don't need is to be left with a hole where a goodbye should have been.
I have met adults in their 50s who still carry that closed door so this is what I would do.
Five minutes.
Not the whole afternoon.
Five minutes with a job.
Bring the water, hold the hand, draw a picture and tape it on the wall where she can see it.
That's the job.
It gives the child something to do with their fear and it gives the person in the bed the one thing that still makes them smile.
The cost is three dollars for crayons and four dollars for tape.
Four dollars and a roll of tape and a child gets to remember that she sang to her grandmother instead of remembering that she was sent
to the other room.
Tonight, think about this week, was a child sent out of the room.
Go and ask that child quietly away from everybody, what did you want to say to her?
And then find the five minutes.
Number six, I would never let my mother think she was a burden.
This is the one that I got wrong.
My mother was Donia Refugio Ibarra.
Cuca, everybody called her.
She raised us in Prospect Hill, a few blocks from Our Lady of Guadalupe.
And she was a woman who could make a meal for 11 people out of nothing and then wash every plate before anybody else stood up.
In March of 2015, she was in her own bed in her own house and I was the one on the chair.
And she started apologizing for the mess in the room, for the smell, for the money, for the nights.
She apologized so much that I stopped hearing it the way you stop hearing the fun in the summer.
One night, around three in the morning, she took my hand and said, in Spanish, Mija, perdóname por todo esto.
Forgive me for all of this, for the trouble.
34 years, almost 3,000 houses.
I had said every kind word to every stranger in this city.
And my own mother was apologizing to me for dying in her own bed.
I sat there with my mouth open.
And what I said was, Mama, you are not a problem.
You have never been a problem.
You are my mother and I would do this for 100 years.
She didn't answer.
She patted my hand twice, the way she did when I was a girl and I had done something foolish.
But I saw her shoulders come down.
I saw it.
That's the only thing I'll take with me from that week, honey.
Her shoulders coming down.
Why do they apologize?
Because they think they have become a cause.
And where do they get that idea?
From us.
From our faces.
From the sigh when she asked for water for the third time.
from the phone we look at while she is talking, from the way we say no it's fine when it is clearly not fine.
So here is the sentence and here is the rest of it.
The sentence is you are not a problem, you are my mother.
The rest of it is that the sentence only works if your face agrees with it.
So take the sigh out of the room, take the money talk out of the room, put the phone in the kitchen face down and don't
bring it back in.
If you're angry at your brother, be angry at your brother in the driveway, not in front of her.
And when she says she's sorry, don't say it's okay.
Look at her, take her hand and tell her what she is.
Tonight, watch yourself, not her.
Watch what your face does when she asks for something for the third time.
She is watching your face, mija.
She has been watching it her whole life.
Number seven, I would never move her out of her own room unless she asked me to.
Mr.
Herman Vogel was my first family in 1991 out in New Braunfels.
A retired man, German, a house that smelled like coffee and wood.
His family had done what so many families do.
They brought in the hospital bed and they set it up in the living room facing the television because that's where there was space.
And one afternoon he asked me to turn him toward the window.
He couldn't do it himself.
He wanted to look at the birds at the feeder his wife had put out years before.
I turned the bed.
It took two of us and it took about four minutes.
And he looked out that window for the rest of the afternoon and didn't say a word.
That was my first lesson in this work, and it came from a man who was living, and it was this.
The bed goes where the life is.
By the last week, most houses have turned into a small hospital.
The pictures come down because there's no room.
The curtains get closed.
The furniture goes against the wall.
The room starts to look like a place where something is happening to a person instead of a place where a person lives.
And I understand why.
There's equipment.
There are people coming and going.
It's easier to clean.
But honey, she is not going to remember the equipment.
She is going to remember the quilt and the light and whose picture is on the wall.
So here's what I did in my mother's room, and what I would do in yours.
The bed goes by the window, so she can see the lemon tree in the patio.
Her own quilt goes on top of the hospice blanket.
Not instead of, on top of, because the blanket is there for a reason, and the quilt is there for her.
The pictures stay up, all of them, even the ones that are crooked.
The little radio goes on the nightstand, on the station she likes, low, and if the room is dark, a lamp, the cheap kind from the
store, $15, on the table, so the light comes from the side and not from the ceiling.
Why does this matter?
I'll tell you exactly why.
Because a room that looks like a hospital tells a person that she is a case, and a room that looks like her room tells her
that she is still home.
and people who are still home.
I have seen this over and over.
They talk more.
They eat a little.
They let you sit with them.
Tonight, go and lie down on that bed, on your back, and look at what she sees.
If the answer is a wall or the back of a television, fix it this week.
It costs less than a pizza, and it is the cheapest thing on this whole list.
Number eight.
I would never let the last conversation be about the schedule.
If you're getting something out of this, do me a favor, hit like and subscribe so this stays where you can find it later and so
the next one in this series finds you.
I'll be here at this table.
My mother's last night was a Thursday.
I remember because Ernie had come by after work, stealing his good shirt from the funeral home, and he sat in the recliner with the radio
on and he did not say one word for two hours.
He just sat there and every so often he reached over and fixed the sheet.
Around 11 everybody went home.
I had a list in my head of things to do in the morning.
Call the agency, call my brother in Laredo, ask about the paperwork, the schedule.
I was standing in the doorway with all of that in my head and I almost said it.
I almost said, Mama, mañana tengo que llamar a la agencia.
Tomorrow I have to call the agency.
34 years.
And the thing in my mouth at 11 o'clock at night was a phone call.
I didn't say it.
I sat down and I said the words I had said to strangers in this city for 34 years and never once to her.
Five sentences.
I forgive you.
Forgive me.
Thank you.
I love you.
Goodbye.
She didn't answer.
She was past answering.
But I said them out loud in her room with my hand in hers so that they were in the air of that house and not
just in my head.
And that is the last thing on my list, not because it's the most beautiful, because it's the one you cannot do later.
You can fix the chairs later, you can buy the lamp later, you can open the binder at any time, but the last conversation does not
wait for you to finish the schedule.
So this is what I would do tonight if I were you.
Take an index card, write five lines on it.
I forgive you, forgive me, thank you, I love you, goodbye.
Put it on the nightstand, under the lamp, where you can see it.
That card costs nothing.
And then, and this is the hard part, figure out which one of the five you cannot say, not which one you like.
Which one makes your throat close?
That's the one you start with tomorrow, because that's the one she's been waiting for.
Now let me bring it all back.
Eight things.
One chair so she isn't a crowd.
A night list on the refrigerator so she isn't alone at two in the morning.
A binder on the kitchen table so the family isn't paying for what is already theirs.
One voice so the arguing happens in the driveway.
Five minutes and a box of crayons so the children get their goodbye.
A sentence and a face that agrees with it so she never thinks she is a ghost.
A bed by the window, so her last room is still her room.
And an index card with five lines on it, so the last thing she hears is not a schedule.
Not one of those things is expensive, not one of them requires a degree.
And I want to say something to you, honey, before you go.
You are not going to do all eight.
I didn't do all eight.
I did six, and I got two wrong, and one of them I got wrong in a way that I still think about at this table
on a Tuesday afternoon.
This list is not a test.
It's a lamp.
It's there so you can see where you are, not so you can be ashamed of where you are.
Because here is what 34 years taught me, and it is the only thing I know for sure.
Nobody does this perfectly.
Not the daughters, not the sons, not the chaplain who has been at it since 1991.
What makes the difference is not doing it right.
It is being in the room.
Be in the room, mija.
That's the whole list.
Now I want to hear from you.
In the comments, tell me who you are taking care of and which one of these eight is the hardest one for you.
I read every comment at this table on Sunday afternoons with a cafecito.
And if you have a question, ask it.
Somebody else in this family of strangers is carrying the same thing tonight.
I put everything I learned in 34 years at the bedside into five books, the last month's playbook, what Medicare's hospice benefit already pays for, and
the words to ask for it, what the last months often look like, and what to say.
The link is in the first line of the description.
And next week, I want to tell you about the morning after.
The first morning when the house is quiet and the bed is empty and there is nothing left to do.
Ernie was there for that one.
He knows that morning better than I do.
I'll see you then.
God bless you, honey.
Go sit with her.
